title: Maths Online Practice Tests & Quizzes for Grade 1 (A Gentle Weekly Plan + Free Quiz)
meta_title: Maths Online Practice Tests for Grade 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: How online maths quizzes help a Class 1 child: instant feedback, short low-pressure bursts, which topics to test, a light weekly plan, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: A six-year-old will happily retry a sum on a screen that they would sulk over on paper. That is the quiet power of a short online quiz — here is how to use maths quizzes well for Grade 1, and how not to, with a free one to try today.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Class 1 child a page of twenty sums and watch what happens around sum number eight: the pencil slows, the eyes drift to the window, and the last five answers are guesses. Six-year-olds do not have the stamina for a long worksheet, and they should not have to. This is exactly where maths online practice tests and quizzes for Grade 1 earn their place. A good quiz is short by design — five or six questions — and it tells the child whether each answer is right the instant they choose it, while the number is still fresh in their head.

That instant feedback is the whole point. It is also easy to get wrong. Used badly, an online quiz becomes just another screen the child zones out in front of. Used well, it turns a five-minute burst into real practice. Here is how I would use quizzes with a six-year-old, which topics actually suit them, and a gentle weekly plan that keeps total screen time to a few minutes a day.

Why a short quiz suits a six-year-old

The maths is the same whether it is on paper or a screen — 8 + 5 is 13 either way. What changes is how a young child responds to it. Three things make a well-made online quiz genuinely helpful at the Grade 1 level:

  • Instant feedback. A tick or a cross appears straight away, so the correction lands while the child still remembers what they did. On a worksheet marked that evening, the moment has passed.
  • Low pressure. There is no red pen and no one watching. A child will cheerfully retry a question they got wrong on a screen, whereas a crossed-out sum on paper can make a six-year-old shut down.
  • Short bursts. A quiz is over in five minutes, which fits a Grade 1 attention span exactly. You can do one before dinner and stop while the child still wants more.

One honest caveat before we go on. A quiz tells you whether a child got the answer, not always how. At this age I still want to see fingers, counters and the odd sum written out, so I know they are reasoning and not just recognising. Use the quiz to catch a slip; use a few counters on the table to check the thinking behind it.

Which Grade 1 topics are worth quizzing

Not every Class 1 topic suits a quick multiple-choice quiz. The ones that do are the number skills a child should slowly come to answer without counting every time. In my experience these are the highest-value Grade 1 topics to practise online:

TopicWhy quiz itExample question
Numbers to 100Counting order and what comes nextWhat comes after 59?
Addition within 20Builds toward fluent recall8 + 5 = ?
Subtraction within 20The trickier direction — needs practice14 − 6 = ?
ShapesNaming circles, squares, trianglesHow many sides has a triangle?
PatternsSpotting what comes next2, 4, 6, 8, ___?
Money (rupees)Real-life and motivating₹5 + ₹2 = ?

Topics I would not lean on quizzes for: anything that needs drawing or handling real objects, like sorting shapes into groups or building a pattern with blocks. A six-year-old learns those with their hands, not by picking an option on a screen. Save those for the kitchen table.

How to use quizzes well — without the screen taking over

The biggest trap with a young child is letting a five-minute tool sprawl into twenty minutes of half-attention. A Grade 1 child does not need a maths app open for that long; that is how you get random tapping and guessed answers. My rule is one short quiz a sitting, once a day is plenty, and stop the moment the child stops thinking.

Sit beside them, not across the room

When a cross comes up, hold your tongue instead of blurting the answer. Ask ‘how did you count that?’ and let them show you on their fingers. That one question teaches more than three more quizzes. Reading the short explanation together after a wrong answer is where the actual learning happens.

Watch for tapping without thinking

If a six-year-old is choosing options in under two seconds, they are tapping, not adding. Cover the screen, put a few buttons or coins on the table, and have them work the sum out for real before they pick. A quiz only helps when the child is genuinely doing the maths.

A gentle weekly quiz plan for Grade 1

Five to ten minutes a day, spread across the week, beats a long weekend session every time — and for a six-year-old, shorter is almost always better. Here is a light structure that has worked for parents I know, one small topic a day with counters or fingers close at hand:

  • Monday: counting and numbers to 100 — a quick quiz, then count aloud together to the next ten.
  • Tuesday: addition within 20 — a short quiz with counters on the table for anything missed.
  • Wednesday: shapes and patterns — a fun, low-stakes quiz to break up the number work.
  • Thursday: subtraction within 20 — the tricky one, so keep it to five questions and use fingers freely.
  • Friday: a mixed quiz covering the whole week, so the child has to notice what each question is asking rather than being told.

That Friday mixed quiz matters most. Practising one skill at a time is easy for a child; realising that this question is an add and that one is a take-away is the real test, and it shows you whether the week actually stuck. Keep weekends free, or fold a tiny bit of maths into real life — counting change from a ₹10 note at the shop, or spotting triangles in the rangoli, both count.

faq.q: Are online quizzes good for a Grade 1 child?
faq.a: Yes, for short bursts on number skills like counting, addition and subtraction within 20, because the instant feedback catches a slip before it sets in and the low-pressure format keeps a six-year-old willing to try again. Keep counters or fingers nearby so you can still see how they reason.

faq.q: How much time should a Class 1 child spend on maths quizzes a day?
faq.a: About five to ten minutes, in a single sitting. One short quiz followed by a quick chat about any wrong answers does far more at this age than a long session that ends in random tapping.

faq.q: How do I stop my child just tapping answers?
faq.a: Sit beside them and ask them to say or show the answer on their fingers before they choose. If they are picking options in under two seconds, cover the screen and put a few coins or buttons on the table so they work it out for real first.

faq.q: Which Grade 1 topics work best as quizzes?
faq.a: Numbers to 100, addition and subtraction within 20, naming shapes, simple patterns and a little money. Skip quizzes for hands-on work like sorting shapes or building patterns with blocks — a six-year-old learns those best with real objects.
